# Improvement loop

The loop's memory between runs. Each run reads this first, picks one item, ships it through the full release sequence in
`CLAUDE.md` onto `main`, which releases it to production (the owner's choice since 2026-10-02), and
updates this file in the same change: add a line to **Shipped**, remove or edit what it resolved, and add any follow-ups
it found. Keep entries short and factual, with numbers where they exist.

| 32     | Progress sync transfers only what is new: `GET /progress/events` returns a cursor (the latest server receipt time it sent), and the app sends it back as `since`, stored with the learner it belongs to, so a sign-in or account switch pulls in full. The server re-reads the last minute before the cursor, since a write stamped earlier can commit after a later read; events are immutable and deduplicated by ID. An account merge now stamps moved events with the merge time, so a device already holding a cursor still receives the guest's history (a test fails without it). New index on learner and receipt time. At the audit's scale (25,000 learners, 3.18 million events) the index builds in 3.2 s, blocking writes to events for that long; for the heaviest learner (4,777 events) a pull of two hours of new events reads 9 buffers in 0.05 ms and 19 kB of payload, against 200 buffers, a sort, 3.8 ms and 755 kB for the full history every visit sent before. An independent review found that two web tabs sharing storage could save a log without an event the other tab's saved cursor had passed, losing it on that device for good; the cursor now lives in the same stored value as the events it covers, so the last writer always leaves a matching pair (the old array format still loads). Browser tests now match progress reads by path, since pulls carry a query. Full browser suite on three profiles against Postgres: 377 passed, one iPhone sign-in test timed out once under load and passed five reruns. | 72     | Behavioral stories sync to a signed-in account; anonymous learners keep them on the device. A new `stories` table (migration 0012, additive) holds each story per account with `updated_at` and a `deleted` tombstone; `GET /api/stories` and `PUT /api/stories/:id` answer accounts only (401 otherwise) and keep the later change per story (a tie keeps the stored copy). The winner is decided on the device's time, and the stored time is no later than the server's clock (so a device running ahead cannot outrank later edits) and after the copy it replaces; the app adopts the stored copy. It blanks a deleted story's text, drops competency ids the catalog no longer has, and refuses NUL and lone surrogates (Postgres cannot store them) with a 400. Limits: 100 live stories (409 `story_limit`, held under the learner's erasure lock so racing writes cannot pass it), the newest 100 tombstones, an 80-character title and 4,000 characters per STAR part (the editor stops there too), 60 reads and 120 writes a minute per account. The app keeps Preferences as the source of truth. Every change is a patch applied in the queue to the stored story, dated after its last change even on a clock that runs behind (engine `nextChange`). An open story follows a change a sync brings in for it, never its own pending saves, and shows a story deleted meanwhile as deleted instead of recreating it; a story emptied for a rewrite stays live, and is deleted only if the learner leaves it blank. A sync pulls, merges (`mergeStories`) and uploads only what is newer, 1.5 s after the last edit, on sign-in, online and visibility (at most every 30 s); it keeps going past a story that fails, stops on offline, 401, 410 or 429, and does not resend a refused story until it changes (a story refused for the limit is retried once a delete is accepted, and on every full pull), naming it and the reason under the bank and on the story. A delete leaves a tombstone only where an account has the story. Signing out uploads what it can; if stories are still missing from the account, the sign-out dialog says how many and that signing out removes them, and nothing is cleared without that choice (when the account cannot be asked, or a tab cannot load the story bank, the dialog says every story on the device could not be checked). Signing in to a different account after a session ended keeps the previous learner's bank aside on the device and brings it back, then uploads it, when that learner signs in here again; signing out and account deletion remove that learner's copy, and it is never exported, as it is device-only. The device is then cleared through the story queue, so no pending write brings the old bank back. Stories join the export and are erased with the account, including a write that arrives during erasure (410). Two adversarial reviews found the silent sign-out loss, stale-page overwrites, the slow-clock and NUL cases, resent refusals, then a blanked story that swallowed later typing and the account switch that wiped unsynced stories; all are fixed with tests. A two-device e2e (write, sign in, second device, edit, delete, export) passed on all three projects A third track, `behavioral`, on the existing `/api/interview` stack (sessions, lease, active-account gate, quota, spend reservations, SSE, mode switch, atomic score, export, erasure), with no migration. Each of the 91 competency questions is a problem (question id, or a competency id for a random question of it) with private notes from the engine (what it checks, strong signals, red flags, follow-ups) and an optional level (early, mid, senior) that sets the bar. The first turn is a STAR answer (5 parts, 4,000 characters each and 12,000 in all, no NUL or lone surrogate), later turns plain follow-up answers; hints, code and a misplaced STAR answer get 400 before any paid work. A bar-raiser prompt, fixed per session so caching holds, asks one to three follow-ups; the answer to the third gets a fixed closing with no model call, quota or reservation (it works with the budget spent), and a fifth turn or any turn after the closing gets 409, so a session makes four quota-counted calls (scoring may retry once). Candidate turns are wrapped in `<candidate_turn>` and our tag names are escaped inside learner text, including lookalikes (format characters, fullwidth brackets, hyphens or spaces). The scorer uses a five-dimension rubric (Competency fit, Ownership & specificity, Impact & results, Judgment & reflection, Follow-up handling) and a schema with `flaws` (id, quote, fix in the candidate's voice) and `weakCompetencies`; normalization keeps a quote only when it is two or more whole words (8+ characters) from one STAR part or follow-up answer (otherwise `quote: null` and a text-free `interview.unquoted-flaw` log), drops unknown ids and clamps the verdict to within one level of the dimension average. Scripted practice asks the question's three follow-ups and scores the STAR checks (capped at 3, unquoted flaws), and is the AI fallback. The engine's `interview.scored` event carries `competencyId` and `weakCompetencies` (the upload schema refuses unknown ones and behavioral weak patterns); progress keeps a `behavioral` slice per competency with `weakSince`, cleared by a later interview on it that does not flag it, and `isDue`/`dueStories` take that slice so a story tagged with a competency flagged since its last telling is due. Also `starFlaws` and an exported `FOLLOW_UP_MIN_WORDS`. New tests fail without the change: engine (progress slice, rehearsal, flaws, follow-up threshold), API unit (prompts, schema, quotes, clamp, scripted branch, request contract, fallback) and an e2e on memory and Postgres (the full session over SSE, free closing, turn rules, flaws into the progress event, guests, budget, upload schema). Live eval scenarios (strong senior, we-heavy, no metric, blame, injection) are added but not run: no API key here. | 77     | System design case studies remember every stage, and finishing one schedules its review. Each stage's answers (the option chosen, the estimate as typed, how many model answer points are open) and the furthest stage are saved on the device as the learner goes (`grasp.case.<id>`, a JSON draft with an attempt id; the older bare furthest-stage number still reads) and restored after a reload, so a decision shows answered with every option's reason and an estimate keeps its value and verdict. Answers stay local like code and STAR drafts (a typed estimate is the learner's own text, and a log of every tap would grow every replay); sign-out and erasure clear them. Reaching the end with every decision and estimate answered records `case.completed` (the case, its design topics, decisions as recommended out of decisions, estimates within 2x out of estimates) with the id `case-<case>-<attempt>`, so recording one run again is deduplicated on the device and by the server, while a run after Start over is a new completion. The reducer keeps `cases` (first date, completions, latest outcome, topics covered), introduces the topics, unlocks their design items (until now only a Design Lab mission did), boosts the first unseen design item of each topic into the next session ahead of the daily cap and pulls scheduled ones to within a day (`CASE_REVIEW_PULL_MS`) unless they were reviewed in the last three days (`CASE_REVIEW_REST_MS`), so several cases in a row do not flood a day, plus 50 XP (10 for a repeat). The event carries the topics so replay does not need the case catalog at startup (3 kB more first paint when the reducer imported it); the API accepts known cases with bounded counts rather than counts matched to the case's current questions, and drops design topics the catalog no longer has (at least one known topic is required), so a later content edit alone does not reject an event recorded before it. The event is recorded from the outcome rather than the tap, so a run whose draft was saved but whose event was not is recorded on its next load. The case list shows Stage N of M for a run in progress (`CaseSummary.stages`, checked against the stages, gives M without loading them) and Finished with the outcome, plus Review and Start over (clears only that case's answers and focuses its first stage) when the answers are on this device. An independent review round then fixed: the outcome (or, while an answer is open, the note with a Go to stage button for the first open stage) takes focus when the case ends, instead of sitting unread above the pitfalls; a saved option index the decision no longer has counts as unanswered instead of locking the case; case drafts held in memory are dropped when local data is cleared (a `cleared` count on the progress service), so a page left open cannot write the previous learner's draft back; Start over's accessible name starts with its visible text; the design topic copy says a finished case also unlocks review items. New tests fail without the change: engine (fold, unlock, pull-forward, session, outcome, stage counts), API (schema and snapshot on memory and Postgres), app (save, restore, the older draft, one completion event, recovery on load, focus at the end, an out-of-range option, clearing, restart) and an e2e (two stages restored after a reload, the list's progress, the event on the real progress endpoint, Finished, Review and Start over); audit states `case-study-in-progress`, `case-study-finished` and `design-list-cases`, clean in both themes on desktop, Pixel 7 and 320 px, and the existing design list and case states match the previous build pixel for pixel. Initial bundle 847.2 kB to 848.9 kB (the reducer, the event type and the draft prefix; the case list and page are lazy). | 81     | Whole AI replies and scoring are bounded (production readiness item 9). Before, the SDK timeout (`ANTHROPIC_TIMEOUT_MS`, 60 s a try) only covered the wait for response headers: a reply stream that kept trickling tokens never ended and held the session's lease for its full 15 minutes, and scoring could run 2 attempts x 3 tries x 180 s (18 minutes) plus backoff before the learner heard anything. A browser disconnect already cancelled the upstream stream. Now a reply, retries and stream included, is cancelled upstream at `INTERVIEW_REPLY_DEADLINE_MS` (default 90 s), combined with the disconnect signal: the learner gets the existing retryable 503 (an SSE `error` once tokens have streamed), neither the candidate's turn nor the partial reply is saved, so the app puts the answer back, spend settles at the input the stream reported plus the output cap (a try cut off before its stream reported anything keeps its hold, as a timeout does), and the lease is released, so a resend works at once. Scoring as a whole, both attempts and every retry, stops at `INTERVIEW_SCORE_DEADLINE_MS` (default 180 s) with the same retryable 503, as before, nothing committed and the charges of calls already made kept, so End & score works again at once; the offline scorecard stays only for two invalid cards, so a slow provider never turns a paid session into a scripted estimate. Scoring is deliberately not cancelled when the learner disconnects: the card commits atomically with its progress event and scoring again returns it without another paid call (25), so cancelling would only waste the spend. Both deadlines are capped at 280 s, so a call ends before Vercel's 300 s function limit could kill it with the lease held (the app waits 190 s for a stream to connect and 290 s for scoring). A deadline is reported only when the error is the abort it caused, so a budget refusal or a 4xx settling after it keeps its own error. New unit tests (fake timers, an endless fake stream, a scorer that never answers, a budget refusal racing the deadline, the config bounds) and HTTP tests (a reply cut at its deadline then resent, a scoring deadline then a score, a mid-stream disconnect) run on memory and Postgres; only the deadline tests get a 1 s interviewer, so the disconnect test fails unless disconnects propagate, and the deadline tests fail on the old code. `npm run verify`: 1,855 app and engine, 402 API unit and 404 API e2e tests (4 skipped) against Postgres. No app change, so the browser suite was not rerun. | 82     | The AI interviewer runs on OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna through the Vercel AI Gateway, the owner's choice after blind-graded comparisons. Run 1 (six models, $0.60) set the field: Claude Sonnet 5.5 passed 94% of the checks at $0.029 billed a session, the cheaper models invented metrics in behavioral fixes (GPT OSS 120B 13, Haiku 4.5 6), which led to `replaceInventedNumbers` (75). Run 3 added GPT-6 Luna and the Grok models: Luna passed 89% (31/35) at $0.0014 billed a session against Sonnet's $0.029, about 1/20th, and repeat 1 held it (90%, 36/40, $0.0013 against $0.0285, 0 invented numbers against Sonnet's 2); every check Luna failed was the cache-read check on behavioral scenarios. In the blind grading of run 3 and repeat 1 it ranked first or near first both times and invented the fewest facts. The switch: `INTERVIEW_AI_PROVIDER` (`gateway` or `anthropic`) defaults to the gateway, and Claude runs only when the owner pins `anthropic` (an Anthropic key alone runs nothing and logs an error). The gateway needs `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` or, on Vercel (`VERCEL_ENV` or `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN`), the deployment's OIDC token, which the gateway accepts as its bearer token and which `@vercel/oidc` reads for every request (from the request's `x-vercel-oidc-token` header, refreshing an expired local one), since it expires; without one, scripted practice, and the log names which runs (`interviewer-choice.ts`, `interviewer.factory.ts`). `INTERVIEW_AI_MODEL` defaults to `openai/gpt-6-luna` (a blank value too), with no fallback model (the owner's decision): an unavailable gateway gets the existing retryable 503 and scripted practice. An `openai/` model is pinned to OpenAI (`providerOptions.gateway.only`), since the disclosure names it. | 91     | Proximity Service, the twenty-fifth system design case study (content idea 4, third piece; core, before Ride Sharing; topics geo, estimation, caching and sharding). Fourteen stages: requirements (the business page shows an edit at once, search may lag a day; distance order only, relevance ranking, reviews and photos out of scope; p99 under 100 ms), search load (100 million daily users × 5 searches, 3x peak: 17,361 searches/s; one page view a search; 1% of 200 million businesses edited a day, 69 edits/s at peak), storage (1 KB a record: 200 GB; a 32-byte index entry: 6.4 GB, so every search server holds the whole index), the API (a page token of the last distance and id and the index version), the spatial index (why a (latitude, longitude) B-tree reads a 4 km band around the planet, about 9,700 times the circle at 40.75° N; fixed grid, geohash, quadtree, S2, H3, R-trees and PostGIS GiST), the build, geohash cells and neighbours, a quadtree for uneven density, filtering by haversine and paging, scaling reads (a full index copy per server and region, cached cell candidates, pages by id through a cache), updates (a nightly versioned snapshot plus incremental batches, loaded beside the old version and switched atomically), sparse places and the nearest K, the antimeridian, the poles and moving users, and failure (validated, canaried snapshots). Two models the learner runs, under `sysdesign/cases/proximity`: a geohash cell search (precision 5 to 7, the user's cell or the cell and 8 neighbours, radius 0.1 to 5 km) over a seeded town of 3,000 places around a user 42 m west of a line where cells split at precision 3 and every finer one, with a place 67 m away across it (sharing 2 characters), reading places, found, missed and read but too far on a map; and a quadtree (10,000 seeded places even, around one city or three cities; leaf capacity 5 to 400) with depth, nodes, places checked and nodes walked by a best-first nearest-20 search, build steps and memory scaled to 200 million (6.9 GB at 100 a leaf around one city). Geohash encode, decode and neighbours and haversine are in the engine, checked against published vectors (u4pruydqqvj, ezs42, the s, e, 7, k quarters, the ngeohash neighbours of dqcjq, Redis's Palermo and Catania), a wrap at 180 degrees, polar cells, and distances from a reference library and the sphere's geometry; the nearest search matches brute force. Each checkpoint is asked from the settings (own cell: what it finds; 9 cells: what they read, or miss when the radius is longer than a side) and has exactly one right, distinct choice of at least three over every slider setting. Readouts that answer a prediction stay hidden until answered, a radius or capacity slider updates them live after an answer while a precision, scope or pattern change asks again, maps are labelled images, one settled summary goes to a persistent status region, and the map's categories use shapes (solid or dashed cell, filled dot, cross, ring, diamond) with a legend. Six review items (cell width by latitude, precision for a radius, distance across a fraction of a degree, the latitude band ratio, the index swap and the nearest-K stop). Lab: 34,800 requests a second at 99.8% reads, no warnings. `npm run verify` exit 0; `proximity-service.spec.ts` 12 of 12 on desktop, Pixel 7 and iPhone (iPhone up to 66 s, marked slow), including both maps at 320 px; case-study, design, feature-flags, payment-ledger and review 14 passed on desktop; audit 12 of 12 clean in each theme (the case, its build and both widgets answered, on desktop, Pixel 7 and 320 px). Initial bundle 852.92 to 853.71 kB (the catalog entry and review summaries); case page chunk 514 to 574 kB. Two independent reviews (facts and teaching, then code and UX) recomputed every figure, confirmed the geohash, haversine, S2, H3 and PostGIS facts, the edge construction and the core tier, and found 12 problems, fixed in a follow-up commit with tests first. Facts: hot cells are a candidate cost, not a lookup cost (split them finer, pre-sort by category, cap candidates, cache only coarse zoomed-out views); intercontinental round trips are about 70 ms (New York to London) to 300 ms (Europe to Australia); open now is checked against the cached record's hours, and the index entry holds only coarse hours; a page token whose index version is gone reruns on the current one; filtered searches widen until 20 matching places lie within the covered distance, with a radius cap; the latitude or longitude range holds hundreds of thousands, not millions; freshness wording; and search servers log coarse cells, not coordinates. Code and UX: dragging the leaf capacity before an answer cost a median 27 to 35 ms a step (p90 34 to 45, max 70 to 86) in Node, since each checkpoint built four neighbour trees and ran 100 nearest-20 queries on each; the build now partitions one shared index array in place, the queue keeps parallel arrays with squared distances, queries run only for the query question (on the two capacity neighbours) and the readouts after an answer, so a step costs a median 5 ms (p90 11 to 12, max 31 to 41). The cells map drew unread places only smaller than found ones (1.12:1); they are now small and faint in the line colour, with their own legend entry, and the too-far ring is thicker. The quadtree map showed the leaves, and so the depth, before the prediction was answered; it now shows only the places until then, then fades them under leaves drawn in the text colour so dense downtown leaves stay visible. | 92     | Production readiness backlog item 12: cohort metrics in SQL, paged feedback, expiring refresh tokens. Measured on a local 25,000-learner fixture (3,287,299 events, heaviest learner 4,775; 7,497 interviews; 9,990 feedback notes; 10,000 accounts with 30,000 sessions and 1,230,000 refresh tokens). **Metrics:** `GET /api/admin/metrics` loaded every event sorted by time into Node (the database sort alone 2.5 s with a 650 MB external sort, the whole report 23 to 28 s and 1.8 to 4.2 GB of memory, far past the pool's 3-second query limit). A `MetricsStore` now has a memory implementation (the unchanged `cohortMetrics`, which stays the reference) and `PostgresMetricsStore`, which computes the same report in five SQL statements in one repeatable-read, read-only transaction and returns only totals: 6.3 to 6.7 s (activity 2.5 s, events 0.5 s, reviews 3.0 to 3.3 s, interviews 0.2 s, feedback 5 ms) and no memory in Node, identical to the reference on the fixture (deep-equal). Learner days and session lengths come from 30-minute bins (a bin never spans a session gap or a UTC midnight), a parallel aggregate over the learner and time index read index-only, so only the 490,535 bins are sorted, not every timestamp; recall sorts review rows in parallel workers before its window. The report has its own 30-second statement and read timeout, since it is operator-only; `jit` and `work_mem` settings changed nothing measurable and were left alone. **Feedback:** `GET /api/admin/feedback` returned every entry; it now returns `{ entries, next }`, newest first by time then ID, 50 by default and at most 200, with an opaque keyset cursor (`?before=`): a page reads 51 rows from the new `feedback (created_at, id)` index in 0.2 ms against a 6.8 ms sort of all 9,990. **Refresh tokens:** nothing deleted them. `sweepExpired` (the existing 10-minute in-process sweeper) now deletes tokens a day past expiry in batches of 5,000 (at most 20 a sweep, `skip locked`), and the session families those deletions leave without a live token, so their access tokens fail `activeFamily`; rotated tokens stay until expiry for reuse detection. The fixture's backlog drained in 8 sweeps of 0.8 to 1.5 s (800,831 tokens and 19,448 families); a steady-state batch finds its rows through the new `refresh_tokens (expires_at)` index in 0.5 ms against a 117 ms sequential scan. Migration `0014` (5-second lock limit) adds both indexes and drops the older `feedback_created_at`; on the fixture it applied in 85 ms for the token index; nothing for the owner to do at release. Tests: a Postgres suite compares the SQL report with the reference on four generated cohorts (timestamps on the 30-minute and one-day thresholds, UTC midnights, future days, legacy drill events, unmetered interviews), hand-built session edges, an empty cohort and a failed query (the connection is discarded); a mutation of the session gap or the recall threshold fails it. Feedback paging is checked on memory and Postgres with ties, inserts between pages (no repeats or gaps), bounds and bad cursors; token sweeping in the auth store contract (both stores) and in `SessionService` (an expired session ends, an active one refreshes). `npm run verify` exit 0 (engine 2,046, API 563 unit and 429 e2e on Postgres, app 596). No page changed, so no browser run. Claude review: no confirmed bugs (bin, session-gap, midnight, recall and percentile equivalence traced by hand; the sweep cannot end a live session; paging and the migration are safe at current scale). Low follow-ups: `feedback.recent` ties order by id in SQL but by insertion in the reference; one malformed legacy interview `at` would fail the whole report; legacy non-UTC `at` offsets land on the UTC day in SQL; repeated operator calls can each hold a pool connection for up to about 150 s (add a single-flight guard); index builds are not `CONCURRENTLY`, fine at pilot sizes. Integration on 32c3214 (no app, engine or e2e change): Playwright 634 passed and 2 iPhone tests timed out in `page.goto` waiting for load (a11y narrow phone, scripted behavioral); both passed 10 of 10 on rerun, another instance of the WebKit follow-up from 86. | 93     | Email Service, the twenty-sixth system design case study (content idea 4, fourth piece; advanced, after Notification System; topics durability, storage, search and queues). Scoped as a consumer mailbox provider at Gmail or Outlook scale, explicitly not a marketing sender. Fourteen stages: requirements (the one promise: never lose mail once 250 is answered), mail flow (500 million daily active mailboxes × 40 received, 2x peak: 462,963 messages/s in; 5 sent a day, 57,870/s out at peak; 263 Gbit/s; 231,481 list loads, 115,741 opens and 23,148 searches a second at peak), storage (1 KB metadata, 20 KB body, 10% with 500 KB attachments: 71 KB a message, 518 PB a year raw; split 7.3, 146 and 365 PB; bodies compressed 3 to 1, 30% attachment dedup assumed: 311 PB, 934 PB in three copies, 467 PB erasure coded; 623 MB a mailbox a year; a search index at 1 KB a message from Lucene's 20 to 30% rule, 14.6 MB a mailbox a year), the client API (202 after a durable write to Sent and the outbound queue, idempotency key; IMAP4rev2/rev1, submission on 587 and 465, JMAP), the data model (metadata sharded by user id, bodies and attachments in a blob store; labels, threads by In-Reply-To and References), the build, receiving (250 only after a write to the inbound queue in two zones; MX, the SMTP conversation, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, ARC, spam and malware, delivery, duplicates, DSNs and backscatter), sending and retries (4xx versus 5xx, RFC 5321 retry guidance, Postfix defaults, IP warm-up, per-domain limits, DKIM signing), content-addressed attachments (SHA-256, sweep-backed deletion, dedup privacy), per-user search indexes with a modseq watermark for just-arrived mail, sync by modification sequence (CONDSTORE and QRESYNC, JMAP state strings and cannotCalculateChanges, push), failure (keep accepting into the queue, 451 when even the queue cannot write, never 550 or removing MX), and transport and rest security (MTA-STS, DANE, TLS-RPT). Two models the learner runs, under `sysdesign/cases/email`: an SMTP retry model (the remote answers 451 or 550 during an outage of 5 minutes to 10 days; first retry 1 to 30 minutes doubling to a longest wait of 30 minutes to 8 hours; queue lifetime 4 hours to 7 days; 20 messages a minute to the domain) showing the outcome and time of a message sent as the outage begins, its attempts, the wait after recovery, the queue at recovery, the bounces and when the queue empties, on a timeline (hatched outage, dashed lifetime, ticks, circle or square); and a storage model (mailboxes, messages a day, attachment share and size, dedup rate, three copies or a 1.5x erasure code) with a year's raw, stored and on-disk bytes, savings, per-mailbox size and quota years, and the split as a solid, striped and dotted bar. The storage model was picked over a search-index model because the metadata versus blob split drives the data-model decision, and its savings show where compression and dedup each apply. Predictions rotate by settings (retry: fate, attempts or drain, a 5xx always asks the fate; storage: largest part, disk or dedup savings); every reachable retry setting (7,680) and a 13,464-setting storage sweep have exactly one right, distinct answer of at least three; the reply and durability radios re-ask, sliders update the readouts live. Closed forms are tested: attempt times against the doubling schedule, delivery and bounce against the first attempt at or after the outage or lifetime, and the queue, bounces and drain against following every message. Per slider step in Node: retry median 0.035 ms (p90 0.16, max 2.9 with warm-up), storage 0.008 ms (max 0.87), so no memoising beyond the computed signals. Eight review items (accept after write, a 451 when the directory is down, retry delivery time and a year of mail and dedup savings from the models, per-user index, sync by modseq, MTA-STS). Lab: one shard group of 5 million mailboxes, 10,100 requests a second at 36% reads, no warnings. `npm run verify` exit 0 (engine 2,083, API 563 unit and 429 e2e, app 603); `email-service.spec.ts` 12 of 12 on desktop, Pixel 7 and iPhone (iPhone up to 1.3 min, marked slow), including both widgets at 320 px; case-study, design, payment-ledger, feature-flags, proximity-service and review 18 passed on desktop; audit 12 of 12 clean in each theme (the case, its build and both widgets answered, on desktop, Pixel 7 and 320 px). Initial bundle 853.71 to 854.07 kB; case page chunk 574 to 636 kB. Unsure facts for the review: Lucene's 20 to 30% index size rule, Gmail's undo send up to 30 seconds and its IMAP labels as folders, and Postfix's 300 to 4,000 second backoff defaults. Two independent reviews (facts and teaching, then code and UX) recomputed every estimate, confirmed the RFCs, enhanced codes, Postfix defaults, Gmail details and the advanced tier, swept all 7,680 retry and 4,488,000 storage settings, and found 10 problems, fixed in a follow-up commit with tests first. Facts: the quota divided 15 GB by deduplicated, compressed bytes while the dedup point charges quota as if stored anew, so quota is now charged at message size (1.04 GB a mailbox a year, about 14 years; `quotaYears` uses raw bytes); waiting out each message's backoff is now presented as the model and Postfix's default, with a large sender releasing a deferred domain's queue at a controlled rate once a delivery or probe succeeds; added a full mailbox (452 4.2.2, then 552 5.2.2, usage counted in the delivery transaction), feedback loops (ARF, RFC 5965), one-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058) and the 0.3% complaint threshold of Gmail and Yahoo's 2024 sender rules, and moving a mailbox between shards by change-log replay. DMARC stays cited as RFC 7489, since no DMARCbis RFC number could be confirmed here. UX: the outage hatching was 1.2:1 against its band (now `--g-muted`, in the drawing and the legend), a short outage drew no hatching (96 of 7,680 settings; the band is now at least 4 units wide), hundreds of attempt ticks merged into a bar (ticks closer than 2 units now show the first 5 and the last with a dotted gap and a legend entry), and a storage part with no bytes drew a sliver (now left out of the bar, its label and the legend). | 94     | Code Deployment System, the twenty-seventh system design case study (content idea 4, its last listed piece; advanced, after Feature Flag Service; topics reliability, observability, CDN and consistency). Scoped as build, deploy and rollout to 50,000 servers in 5 regions, explicitly not a CI test runner. Fifteen stages: requirements (a bad release caught on a small known slice and rolled back automatically, every server on a recorded release), the deploy rate (2,000 services × 4 a day = 8,000; busiest hour 3x: 1,000 an hour, 0.28/s; 100,000 instance updates an hour; about 3,750 rollouts in flight by Little's law), the fan-out (20,000 servers × 500 MB = 10 TB from one 10 Gbit/s origin: 8,000 s, 133 min; 400 TB a day company-wide, 37 Gbit/s average), the deploy API (a digest, an environment, a plan and an idempotency key, recorded as desired state, 202), deployments and locks (one active deployment per service by compare-and-set, a state machine, leases with fencing), the Lab build, build once (hermetic and reproducible builds, content-addressed cache, signed in-toto provenance, SLSA 1.0 build levels, admission, secrets out of the artifact), distribution (regional caches, peer to peer with Twitter's Murder, Facebook's BitTorrent use, Kraken and Dragonfly, piece hashes, deltas by layers, chunking and Courgette, pre-staging), rollout in waves (rolling with Kubernetes' 25% defaults labelled as defaults, blue-green, canary, waves by failure domain, bake; an estimate of 225 min for a 1% canary, 4 equal waves, 30-minute bakes, 5% out at once, 5 min a batch), health and canary analysis (a same-size, same-age baseline, Kayenta's Mann-Whitney U, statistical caveats, rollback triggers, max unavailable and surge, error budgets, freezes), desired state (idempotent pulling agents, stragglers and dead hosts, stuck rollouts with deadlines, the control plane down mid-rollout: hosts keep their release), schema changes (expand and contract, forward-only data migrations, gh-ost), config versus code and flags (linking the Feature Flag case), and failure (a poisoned cache refused by the signed digest, bad agent releases, leaked signing keys). Two models the learner runs, under `sysdesign/cases/deploy`: a rollout plan (fleet 100 to 20,000, canary 0.5 to 10%, 1 to 6 waves equal or doubling, bake 0 to 2 h, 1 to 25% out at once, 1 to 15 min a batch, detection 5 min to 2 h after the canary serves) with total time, peak capacity out and the hosts a bad build reaches before the alarm, on a step chart (solid line, dashed alarm, circle); and artifact distribution (sizes 50 MB to 5 GB, 100 to 50,000 hosts, origin 1 to 100 Gbit/s, 0 to 20 regional caches, peer to peer and a 10% delta) from the Kumar and Ross fluid bounds (N × F / server upload; F / seed, N × F / (seed + N × peer upload), F / download), the slowest tier setting the time, with origin egress and the bottleneck as bars (solid for the bottleneck, outlined otherwise, a tier with no caches left out). Predictions rotate by settings (rollout: duration or blast radius; distribution: time, bottleneck only when the runner-up needs at most 80% of its time, or origin egress); a 204,120-setting rollout sweep (every stop of every slider, fleet and batch time at ends and the example) and all 9,408 distribution settings have exactly one right, distinct answer of at least three; the closed forms match a batch-by-batch stepper and the textbook bounds, and a bake at least as long as detection keeps a bad build in the canary. The wave shape and the peer and delta radios re-ask; sliders update live. Per slider step in Node: rollout median 0.02 ms (p90 0.05, max 9.9 on the first, cold call; 0.9 warm), distribution median 0.02 ms (max 0.8). Eight review items (blast radius and rollout duration from the model, fan-out time, peer-to-peer scaling, expand and contract, desired state, canary baseline, digest verification). Lab: the control plane, 50,000 agents polling every 30 s and reporting every 60 s, 2,500 requests a second at 66% reads, no warnings. `npm run verify` exit 0 (engine 2,121, API 563 unit and 429 e2e, app 61 files); `code-deployment.spec.ts` 12 of 12 on desktop, Pixel 7 and iPhone (iPhone up to 1.3 min, marked slow), including both widgets at 320 px; case-study, design and review 9 passed on desktop; audit 12 of 12 clean in each theme (the case, its build and both widgets answered, on desktop, Pixel 7 and 320 px). Initial bundle 854.07 to 854.43 kB. Unsure facts for the review: Facebook's BitTorrent distribution of its web binary, Kayenta's Mann-Whitney U judge, the SLSA 1.0 level wording, and Twitter's Murder. Two independent reviews (facts and teaching, then code and UX) confirmed every figure, the fluid bounds, the lower-bound labels and those four facts, swept all 1,088,640 rollout and 9,408 distribution settings clean, and found 11 problems, fixed in a follow-up commit with tests first. Facts: the rollout-duration review item always said bake time was most of it (now whichever of baking or updating is longer); surge is described as maxUnavailable 0 with a surge, the defaults allowing 25% down; added deploy dependencies between services (compatible both ways, provider first, gated on its rollout completing), rolling forward when rollback is unsafe, monorepo builds by reverse dependencies, rotating secrets with overlap, unconverged hosts drained and repaired, and the 3,750 rollouts in flight worded as an upper bound at the busiest rate. UX: tiers under 2% of the slowest drew 3 px bars that were all border (now at least 6 px with a 1 px outline), the bottleneck question offered the regional caches with none present (now only tiers present, padded to three with the control plane's API), and the alarm's legend says no batch starts from it. | 95     | Production readiness backlog item 13: public reads without counter writes, and pooled connections measured. **Found:** the stable public reads are `GET /api/auth/config` (the only one the app calls, on the sign-in options) and the six curriculum lists (`patterns`, `algorithms`, `drills`, `topics`, `review-items`, `scenarios`; the app bundles that content and does not call them). None was cacheable: `auth/config` sent `no-store` and wrote a per-address counter; the curriculum lists sent no `Cache-Control`, read the learner's account link and wrote two counters (learner and network) per anonymous request. `/api/health` already skipped both. **Change:** a `@PublicRead()` decorator (`common/public-read.ts`) skips the identity guard and the rate-limit counter and sends `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, s-maxage=3600, stale-while-revalidate=86400`; Express's existing weak ETag (a body hash) gives 304s, Vercel's CDN cache key includes the deployment so a release never serves an older copy, and the only `Vary` is CORS's `Origin` (tested: the native and web origins each get their own `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`). Public responses drop `x-request-id`, so a cached copy carries no caller's id (the server log keeps it). A request carrying `Authorization` gets `no-store` (Vercel never caches it anyway); learner-specific routes keep `no-store`. The random review question, `POST .../trace`, writes, AI and auth routes keep their limits. **Measured** on a local production build against local Postgres, 100 keep-alive clients for 20 s, a fresh learner id and address per request: `GET /api/curriculum/patterns` 842 to 2,034 requests/s, p50 115 to 46 ms, p99 175 to 93 ms, 2.94 to 0 database statements and 1.95 to 0 row writes a request; `topics` 1,172 to 3,274/s (p50 83 to 28 ms, p99 118 to 57 ms), same writes; `auth/config` 2,568 to 3,835/s (p50 38 to 24 ms, p99 63 to 49 ms), 0.97 to 0 writes; `health` unchanged (6,000 and 5,431/s, noise). These are cache misses; on Vercel a CDN hit does not reach the function at all. A still-counted route afterwards: 743/s, 1.90 writes, 10 pool connections busy. **Pool:** `max: 10` per instance, pg's 10-second idle close, `attachDatabasePool`; six local instances under load held 60 connections (instances × 10). Against Neon's PgBouncer (10,000 clients, 0.9 × `max_connections` server connections: 94 at 0.25 CU) that is about 1,000 warm instances; the direct endpoint (104 at 0.25 CU) fails at about 10, so the API now warns at startup on a Neon direct host. `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` documents the model. The app has no service worker and fetches with `cache: 'no-store'`, so nothing it reads goes stale; `npm run verify` passes, and the sign-in and interview e2e specs pass on all three projects (45 passed, 3 skipped). Claude security review: no confirmed issues (no per-caller variation, no Set-Cookie, `Vary: Origin` emitted and honoured, Authorization bypasses the cache, the identity skip is safe). Integration: Playwright 659 passed on 117c97a with 1 iPhone retention failure from a `WPENetworkProcess` segfault in libgobject confirmed in dmesg (the Playwright WebKit crash from 86); e444230 | 96     | Three Design Lab missions on the recent case studies, nine in all, and the object store's traffic share moves into the workload. **Object share:** `Workload.objectShare` (the share of requests that upload or fetch whole files) replaces the object store's node setting, so a mission fixes it and a learner can no longer send any share they like to a $500 store. Free and case builds set it with a Files slider in the workload panel (the inspector slider is gone); until a share is named it reads "old rule (N%)", with the thumb at the share the board runs at (`legacyObjectShare`: the first store linked from the first app that links one, 30% if it saved none), and new free builds name 30%. Missions show it on their card and brief ("50% files"). When a workload names its share, the simulator tracks files through the board: an app, a CDN or workers send every file they carry to a connected object store and nothing else, so files diverted at a CDN are not counted again at the app, and records cannot be parked in a store. Workers left holding records with no database fail them ("Workers have no database for records"). Before, a queue whose workers wrote only to an object store cleared The Write Wall for $5,650, and a CDN linked to a store took half of all writes. Boards that name no share keep the old rule (from apps, the share saved on their first store, 30% by default; an instance-count split at CDNs and workers): all 27 case builds compare equal field by field. A saved board is never rewritten on load (`restoreBoard`, free, case and mission alike): a board saved before 96 keeps the share on its stores, the old rule reads it, and only the learner moving the Files slider converts it (`nameObjectShare` strips the node shares and names the workload's); missions hide the slider, so an old mission board stays on the old rule, including a share the old inspector let the learner set. An adversarial re-review then found eight more, all fixed: an idle queue's workers inflated the drain rate (queues now drain from what they hold, a worker shared by several queues is spent once, and the drain time is that of the slowest group of queues sharing workers, so an idle queue beside a full one adds nothing), one replica node under several primaries counted for each of them (it can no longer be connected to a second database, and on an old board it counts for none and says so), the two-app-tier migration exception, the storm's hint and takeaway blaming the write rate rather than the worker size (one worker drains 1,500 a second, too slow; two send 6,000 ops a second, more than one primary's 5,000), the Files slider not saving on its own, `DEFAULT_OBJECT_SHARE` moving to a dependency-free `object-share.ts`, and the failover twist. A third adversarial round then found that the greedy worker split still let an idle queue linking the busy worker to a spare one clear Reconnect Storm with one primary, and that the result depended on the order links were drawn (a Write Wall board passed or failed by edge order). Queues now drain by the exact fluid model (`queue-drain.ts`): over the queues holding work, the set with the most load per unit of worker capacity it can reach is peeled off, its workers serve it at one utilization, and so on (Hall's theorem; a maximum flow assigns queue to worker), so backlog is the least any assignment reaches, the drain time is the slowest block's, idle queues add nothing, and any order of nodes and links gives the same metrics (a property test shuffles them). Old-rule workers with stores and no database send everything to the stores (six or more stores showed a false critical insight), the storm's takeaway is version-neutral with the base arithmetic in hint 3, revisit 1's story fits the one fleet, the shared-replica wording counts databases ("One replica node copies N databases"), and an app spec now walks the titles chunk's imports and fails if they reach the component catalog (it fails with 066d0d6's files). Budgets re-searched again: unchanged. A fourth adversarial round found eleven more (G0 to G10), all fixed. Thirteen or more busy queues were pooled into one block, so The Write Wall passed with one primary behind thirteen queues and a queue with no worker showed no backlog, and enumerating subsets made a simulate up to 50 times slower at 12 queues: the densest set is now found exactly within each group of queues sharing workers by Dinkelbach's method (a parametric maximum flow, source to queue at its load, queue to worker, worker to sink at the trial ratio times its capacity; the maximal source side of the minimum cut is the next set, until the ratio stops rising), exact ratios of sums with a tolerance only for comparisons, and a queue no worker can reach is its own block that never drains. A spec checks it against exhaustive enumeration on 1,000 random boards of up to 10 queues (blocks, growth, drain ratio and every worker's load), and a board of 20 queues and 40 workers simulates in about 5 ms (0.9 ms at the parent, whose greedy split was wrong; the case builds take 89 µs against 70). Which queue feeds which worker no longer depends on the order links were drawn (the maximum-flow split did, so worker loads, the files they carried and the database load flipped, and a mail revisit passed or failed by link order): within a block the flow is the unique scaling of its links to the queue and worker totals (iterative proportional fitting over sorted ids), and worker carry and link labels use it; the shuffle property test now also covers boards whose queues carry different shares of files under a named share, in both link orders, and every reference design, comparing node and link loads, metrics and goal checks. Insights keep the board's topological order though workers are worked out last (two critical insights had swapped on a single-queue board), the `objectShare` doc says absence selects the old rule, Files at 100% with workers writing only to the store no longer raises a false "no database for records", storm revisits 2 and 3 name their outages, the Attachments takeaway no longer says "here half the shards", and the Files thumb on an old board sits at the share the board runs at (an old File Sync build at 50%, not 30%; the e2e board at 70). In a column run (a table, or a graph or tree under an array) the stage is a column of fixed height (`.viz.column`): the drawing starts at its full-width height and takes what the views above it, its legend on as many lines as it wraps to and a 66px first row of the lists leave; a table (`.fit`, a size container) goes down to cells 1.6 times their text and as wide as their column labels, with its row labels counted in the width, and its square cells shrink to the box; an array above keeps room for the run's most pointer rows (`band`, `pointerRowsOf`), so the drawing keeps one size on every frame. The iteration 18 browser replay found that Chromium cached a `410 learner_erased` response by URL and replayed it after a
fresh learner ID was stored. The follow-up sets `no-store` for learner-specific API responses and app requests,
and checks that a fresh event survives another reload.

## Production readiness backlog

The local audit of `4beccbd` used an isolated Postgres fixture with 25,000 learners and 3.18 million events. Its 200-client runs found no ordinary-route errors, but failure probes found the risks below. Work through the remaining iterations in order before a wider release.

| Iteration | Status                             | Work                                                                                                             |
| --------- | ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1         | Done in 17                         | Require Postgres in production, refuse traffic without its URL, and recover after an idle connection drops.      |
| 2         | Done in 17                         | Bound database connect and query waits, return 503 for dependent routes, and let learners retry timed-out calls. |
| 3         | Done in 18                         | Make account deletion atomic against in-flight interviews and revoke old access tokens across instances.         |
| 4         | API 19; JS 20; native P0           | Keep learner text, IDs and tokens out of database error logs and Sentry envelopes.                               |
| 5         | 21/22/23; shared-network limits 68 | Require active accounts for paid AI and improve anonymous shared-network limits.                                 |
| 6         | Migrations rehearsed in 33         | Gate hand deploys on CI, rehearse additive migrations and restore, and roll back failed postflights.             |
| 7         | Done locally in 24                 | Retain clock-skewed progress until accepted and split offline batches below the body limit.                      |
| 8         | Atomic score 25; reconnect sync 69 | Sync active devices on reconnect and visibility; atomic score completion is implemented locally.                 |
| 9         | Done in 81                         | Bound whole AI streams and scoring, and cancel upstream work when clients disconnect.                            |
| 10        | Done in 85                         | Alert on grouped slow-database and AI failures without logging every success or private data.                    |
| 11        | Cursor pull done in 32             | Add cursor-based progress sync and a bounded local checkpoint instead of replaying full history on every visit.  |
| 12        | Done in 92                         | Aggregate cohort metrics without a global event sort; paginate feedback and expire old refresh tokens.           |
| 13        | Done in 95                         | Cache stable public reads without counter writes and measure pooled connections across many warm instances.      |
| 14        | P2                                 | Version and compress Pyodide, and cache safe startup responses. Component route warming is bounded in 23.        |
| 15        | P2, P3                             | Export all account data, mark private reads `no-store`, and prompt stale tabs to reload safely.                  |

## Open follow-ups

- The production audit cannot finish from the build container: both themes stop at the 50-minute limit after about 210 states, and a few states time out on first load through the proxy (rechecked clean). Split the production audit by state group or run it from CI.
- `apps/api/src/interview/gateway.interviewer.spec.ts` "cancels a reply still streaming at its deadline" is flaky: it failed 1 run in 3 alone during iteration 96 (which does not touch it). Find the timing race and fix it; never skip it.
- Iterations 19 to 25 were built by Codex on `feature/improvements-codex` and fast-forwarded into `feature/improvements` after an independent Claude review; iteration 26 on continues there without Codex. The owner clarified the capacity target as 100,000 simultaneous active users. Its priority is production readiness for that concurrency, followed by deeper, reviewed algorithms and system-design lessons and practice. Registered-account counts and local rehearsals do not prove this target; wider-release claims require a defined workload and distributed production-like measurements. The owner excludes older-client compatibility from new work; preserve existing learner data without adding legacy transport paths.
- JavaScript Sentry reporting now uses an explicit capture and transport allowlist. Native crash uploads are temporarily disabled because JavaScript callbacks cannot filter native envelopes. Restore them only with native filtering and crash/relaunch, offline replay and prior-cache verification. The API uses explicit sanitized reports only, so automatic unhandled-process Sentry capture is disabled.
- Before promoting iteration 21, drain or disable all older paid API instances, finish their provider calls and protect older deployment URLs. The additive ledger migration imports old totals, but old code cannot see reservations or new charges. Rolling back to old admission logic requires disabling paid traffic. Conservative full-context reservations also require headroom for concurrent attempts; see `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md`.
- Iteration 22 changes route counter keys and authentication limits. During a mixed-version rollout, route allowances split and older instances retain small per-IP auth buckets. Retire them before relying on classroom fairness. The 1,200-per-minute network cap is per auth endpoint and still allows fixed-window bursts; the local 1,000-account rehearsal is not production capacity certification. Public anonymous routes still share their existing per-IP buckets. Iteration 23 closes guest paid access through verified accounts and explicit AI selection; account deletion/recreation and additional verified accounts are not one-human entitlement controls.
- Third-party console logging still needs review: the installed social-login plugin logs raw storage parse errors, and Capacitor logs raw bridge failures. The application-owned error handlers and outbound Sentry reports are filtered; do not claim every dependency console message is private.

Known issues and deferred work, most valuable first.

- Failure signals after 85: the four Sentry alert rules exist (created 2026-10-01); no signal has reached a real Sentry project, so check the first production one (its tags, fingerprint and `failures`). Grouping is per instance: failures held back in a window reach Sentry only with that instance's next failure of the signal, so a recycled instance loses them, and Sentry's event count is instance-windows, not failures. The persistence sweep records no signal. `ai.failed` now reaches Sentry only as a signal, without the stack of the bug behind it; if that hides a real bug, report `ai.failed` causes one by one again. A bare network error from a non-database call that escapes to the filter would read as `db.unavailable`. Sign-in provider outages (Google, GitHub 503s) are logged warnings with no signal or alert; add an `auth.provider` signal if they matter. Server `statement_timeout` (above) would turn a stuck query into a `db.timeout` signal instead of a client-side one.
- Retention e2e specs under load (84): two iPhone progress-sync retention tests failed while the machine also ran `npm run verify`, the test's direct `GET /progress` getting a 503 from a rate limit counter store timeout; they passed 80 of 80 on a quiet machine. Make the specs and the Postgres rate limit store robust under load (the store now signals `rate-limit.store`). 86 logged no counter store timeout over about 1,000 browser tests at load averages up to 21, so it needs the heavier `npm run verify` load to reproduce.
- GPT-6 Luna (82) has not met the new prompts: run the live eval and the comparison against it
  (`AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY=... MODELS=openai/gpt-6-luna npm run eval:models`; needs a key) and blind-grade the transcripts for one
  question a turn, hidden-material mentions, praise and markdown. Repeats 2 and 3 of the repeat test were run but not graded.
  Luna reported no cache reads on any behavioral scenario (its only failed checks), likely because the behavioral prompt is under
  OpenAI's 1,024-token caching minimum; that costs money, not quality. The first production AI call should confirm that the
  function's request context carries `x-vercel-oidc-token` with `NODEJS_HELPERS=0` (a missing token logs `ai.rejected`
  with a 401); confirm it by the first production log line and one real reply. Streamed deltas still show the model's raw text until the SSE `done` message replaces it with the normalized reply.
  Session usage records the catalog cost at base rates; the spend ledger holds the billed one. Every cold start fetches the
  catalog (up to 5 s before the first request on that instance; the built-in prices cover an outage).

- The AI behavioral interviewer (74) shipped dark, and the app offers it since 76. Before release: run the live eval with a key (its five
  behavioral scenarios have never met the real model, so the prompts, the flaw quotes and the reply length are unmeasured);
  and have the owner confirm the Settings disclosure wording that STAR answers go to OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna through Vercel's AI Gateway (82). Whole replies and scoring
  are bounded since 81 (90 s and 180 s by default); check those against the live eval's timings. The
  verdict clamp to within one level of the dimension average applies to behavioral scorecards only; coding and design
  scorecards still trust the model's verdict, and the same clamp would suit them. An unknown `competencyId` fails the
  whole progress upload, so renaming a catalog competency needs a migration path for stored events.
- The app track (76) disclosure is settled: Settings and the pilot notice share one text in `core/ai-disclosure.ts` ("your interview messages, shared code and behavioral answers, including any story you start an answer from, are sent to OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna through Vercel's AI Gateway" since 82), and the provider name there is the one line to change if the interviewer's provider changes, including `INTERVIEW_AI_PROVIDER=anthropic`. A scorecard
  offers Add to story bank unless the answer started from a story in this app session or equals a story in the bank, so
  after a reload an edited story-started answer is offered again. The session keeps the model's own early closing
  (a thank-you before the third follow-up) open for another answer; only the server's closing disables the composer.
- Left open from the 76 review: an answer drafted on `/behavioral/question/:id` is not offered in the session its entry
  starts; the Rehearse queue is a snapshot taken on entering the page, so on a fresh device it can be taken before the
  progress pull brings in a flag; Add to story bank disables the button that has focus, as the mock does; and when the
  scripted interviewer closes early (a question removed since the session started) the composer stays open and the next
  send gets a plain 409 until the session reloads. The app has no local 100-story limit on Add to story bank; the
  account refuses the 101st and the bank names the refusal.
- Story sync (72) sends one request per story: a first sign-in with a full bank of 100 makes 100 PUTs, inside the
  120-a-minute limit. Past 100 deletes, a device that still holds a very old copy can bring a deleted story back. New
  story ids are the creation millisecond in base 36, so two devices creating a story in the same millisecond would share
  one; switch to random ids if that ever shows up. Refusals are remembered for the app session only, so a reload sends
  a refused story once more. An expired bank kept aside (73) is dropped only when the story bank first loads or that
  learner signs in, so a device that never opens a behavioral page again keeps it until then. A device clock running fast wins once over an edit made later in real time elsewhere (the winner is
  the device's own time; the stored stamp is clamped, so it wins only once). Reviving a story deleted elsewhere while
  the page's own save is still pending keeps only the edited part. The export reads the account, so it cannot rescue stories that never
  reached it.
- A signed-in page that reloads pulls progress by device id before its session renews, so the API answers 401 once and
  the browser logs it (the story sync e2e expects it). Waiting for the renewal, or sending the stored token, would avoid it.

- The pull overlap assumes event writes finish within a minute. The API gives up on a query after 3 s, but Postgres keeps
  running it: no server-side `statement_timeout` or `lock_timeout` is set outside the spend store. A single-row insert
  stuck on a lock for over a minute could commit behind a device's cursor. Set server timeouts on the pool once the Neon
  pooler is confirmed to accept them.
